title: Facebook whistleblower behind 'The Social Reckoning' says Zuckerberg is ‘playing with fire’ on AI
key_facts: Fortune interviewed Frances Haugen, the Facebook whistleblower of 2021, as Aaron Sorkin's film The Social Reckoning opens in US cinemas this week.
Haugen calls Mark Zuckerberg's AI push 'playing with fire', driven by a wish for a positive legacy.
She does not back a pause in AI development: 'Slowing down just means whoever doesn't want to slow down wins.'
She backs independent auditors, part of Dario Amodei's recent plan for third-party evaluators with 'employee-like access'; Sam Altman said OpenAI would do the same; she wants it required by law.
She has not seen a culture change at Meta; Meta did not reply to Fortune's request for comment before press time.
She expects even very advanced AI to catch only 10% to 20% of harmful content, against about 5% when she left.
quote_evidence: “We have never done a prohibition where we could properly check,” she said. “Slowing down just means whoever doesn’t want to slow down wins.”
Haugen says the best mitigation to AI harms is for this kind of auditing to be required by law across the industry, the way outside auditors are entitled to review the books at banks.
(Fortune contacted Meta for comment on Haugen’s claims but the company did not reply before press time.)
why_it_matters_hint: A well-known tech whistleblower argues for legally required outside audits of AI labs rather than a pause.
